items.readable_text:
Content:
In the previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms directly from the definition,
[MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,\textrm d t,]
where [MATH: s] is a real number.

Content:
So far, the following basic transforms have been computed:

Content:
| [MATH: f(t)] | [MATH: F(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}] | Domain |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{s}] | [MATH: s > 0] |
| [MATH: e^{kt}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{s-k}] | [MATH: s > k] |
| [MATH: e^{\textrm i \omega t}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{s-\textrm i \omega}] | [MATH: s > 0] |

Content:
Of course, not every function will appear in a table. Fortunately, the Laplace transform has a linearity property, which lets us break complicated functions into simpler pieces.

Content:
For functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] the linearity property states that
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\}
= \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L\{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

Content:
Watch out: Laplace transforms do not distribute over products. In general,
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\,g(t) \right\} \ne \mathcal{L}\left\{ f(t) \right\}\,\mathcal{L}\left\{ g(t) \right\}.]

Content:
Finally, when we apply linearity, the Laplace transform of the overall function exists only where every piece exists. So the domain of
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\}]
is the intersection of the domains of [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] and [MATH: \mathcal L\{g(t)\}.]

Content:
In the next slide, we will apply the linearity property to a concrete example.

items.title: Finding Laplace Transforms of Sums of Exponentials

sections.normalized_html: Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{-3t}-e^{5t}] for [MATH: s>5.]
sections.readable_text: Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{-3t}-e^{5t}] for [MATH: s>5.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have [MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},] where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have [MATH: L{e^{− 3t} − e^{5t}}|= L{e^{− 3t}} + L{− e^{5t}}; = L{e^{− 3t}} − L{e^{5t}}.]

Next, we recall the following result: [MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k]

Therefore, we have the following: [MATH: L{e^{− 3t}}|= (1)/(s + 3), s > − 3; L{e^{5t}}|= (1)/(s − 5), s > 5]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)] is [MATH: L{f(t)}|= L{e^{− 3t}} − L{e^{5t}}; = (1)/(s + 3) − (1)/(s − 5); = ((s − 5) − (s + 3))/((s + 3)(s − 5)); = (− 8)/((s + 3)(s − 5)); = − (8)/((s + 3)(s − 5)).]

Finally, since [MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{-3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (-3,\infty)] and [MATH: \mathcal L \{e^{5t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (5,\infty),] we have that [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] is defined for [MATH: (-3,\infty) \cap (5,\infty) = (5,\infty),] that is, [MATH: s > 5.]

Example Prompt:
Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{-3t}-e^{5t}] for [MATH: s>5.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have
[MATH: L{e^{− 3t} − e^{5t}}|= L{e^{− 3t}} + L{− e^{5t}}; = L{e^{− 3t}} − L{e^{5t}}.]

Next, we recall the following result:
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k]

Therefore, we have the following:
[MATH: L{e^{− 3t}}|= (1)/(s + 3), s > − 3; L{e^{5t}}|= (1)/(s − 5), s > 5]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)] is
[MATH: L{f(t)}|= L{e^{− 3t}} − L{e^{5t}}; = (1)/(s + 3) − (1)/(s − 5); = ((s − 5) − (s + 3))/((s + 3)(s − 5)); = (− 8)/((s + 3)(s − 5)); = − (8)/((s + 3)(s − 5)).]

Finally, since [MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{-3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (-3,\infty)] and [MATH: \mathcal L \{e^{5t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (5,\infty),] we have that [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] is defined for
[MATH: (-3,\infty) \cap (5,\infty) = (5,\infty),]
that is, [MATH: s > 5.]

items.title: Finding the Laplace Transform of Cosine Using Linearity

sections.normalized_html: We will find the Laplace transform of [MATH: \cos(t)] by rewriting it using complex exponentials and applying linearity.

items.readable_text:
Content:
We will find the Laplace transform of [MATH: \cos(t)] by rewriting it using complex exponentials and applying linearity.

Content:
First, we recall the identity
[MATH: \cos(t) = \dfrac{e^{\mathrm{i} t} + e^{-\mathrm{i} t}}{2}.]

Content:
Now, we take the Laplace transform of both sides:
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\cos(t)\}
= \mathcal L\left\{\dfrac{e^{\mathrm{i} t} + e^{-\mathrm{i} t}}{2}\right\}.]

Content:
Next, we apply linearity:
[MATH: L{\cos (t)}|= (1)/(2)L{e^{\textrm{i}t} + e^{− \textrm{i}t}}; = (1)/(2)(L{e^{\textrm{i}t}} + L{e^{− \textrm{i}t}}).]

Content:
From the previous lesson, we know that for [MATH: s>0,]
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-\mathrm{i} \omega}.]
So for [MATH: \omega=1,] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{\mathrm{i} t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-\mathrm{i}},
\qquad
\mathcal L\{e^{-\mathrm{i} t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s+\mathrm{i}}.]

Content:
Substituting these into our expression gives
[MATH: L{\cos (t)}|= (1)/(2)((1)/(s − \textrm{i}) + (1)/(s + \textrm{i})); = (1)/(2)(((s + \textrm{i}) + (s − \textrm{i}))/((s − \textrm{i})(s + \textrm{i}))); = (1)/(2)((2s)/(s^{2} − \textrm{i}^{2})); = (1)/(2)((2s)/(s^{2} + 1)); = (s)/(s^{2} + 1).]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\cos(t)\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+1}, \qquad s>0.]

sections.normalized_html: Use the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{kt}] to find the Laplace transform of [MATH: \sinh(3t).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have [MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},] where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

First, recall that, by definition [MATH: \sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.]

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have [MATH: L{\sinh (3t)}|= L{(e^{3t} − e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = L{(e^{3t})/(2) − (e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = L{(e^{3t})/(2)} − L{(e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = (1)/(2)L{e^{3t}} − (1)/(2)L{e^{− 3t}}.]

Now, we recall that [MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.] Therefore, we have the following: [MATH: L{e^{3t}}|= (1)/(s − 3), s > 3; L{e^{− 3t}}|= (1)/(s + 3), s > − 3]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: \sinh(3t)] is [MATH: L{\sinh (3t)}|= (1)/(2)L{e^{3t}} − (1)/(2)L{e^{− 3t}}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(s − 3) − (1)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(s + 3); = (1)/(2)((1)/(s − 3) − (1)/(s + 3)); = (1)/(2)(((s + 3) − (s − 3))/((s − 3)(s + 3))); = (1)/(2)((6)/(s^{2} − 9)); = (3)/(s^{2} − 9).]

Finally, since [MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (3,\infty)] and [MATH: \mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (-3,\infty),] we have that [MATH: \mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}] is defined for [MATH: (3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),] that is, [MATH: s > 3.]

[MATH: (3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),]
that is, [MATH: s > 3.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

First, recall that, by definition
[MATH: \sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.]

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have
[MATH: L{\sinh (3t)}|= L{(e^{3t} − e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = L{(e^{3t})/(2) − (e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = L{(e^{3t})/(2)} − L{(e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = (1)/(2)L{e^{3t}} − (1)/(2)L{e^{− 3t}}.]

Now, we recall that
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.]
Therefore, we have the following:
[MATH: L{e^{3t}}|= (1)/(s − 3), s > 3; L{e^{− 3t}}|= (1)/(s + 3), s > − 3]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: \sinh(3t)] is

Finally, since [MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (3,\infty)] and [MATH: \mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (-3,\infty),] we have that [MATH: \mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}] is defined for
[MATH: (3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),]
that is, [MATH: s > 3.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In the previous lesson, we learned how to compute Laplace transforms directly from the definition,
[MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,\textrm d t,]
where [MATH: s] is a real number.

Content:
So far, the following basic transforms have been computed:

Content:
| [MATH: f(t)] | [MATH: F(s)=\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}] | Domain |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{s}] | [MATH: s > 0] |
| [MATH: e^{kt}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{s-k}] | [MATH: s > k] |
| [MATH: e^{\textrm i \omega t}] | [MATH: \dfrac{1}{s-\textrm i \omega}] | [MATH: s > 0] |

Content:
Of course, not every function will appear in a table. Fortunately, the Laplace transform has a linearity property, which lets us break complicated functions into simpler pieces.

Content:
For functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] the linearity property states that
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\}
= \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L\{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

Content:
Watch out: Laplace transforms do not distribute over products. In general,
[MATH: \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\,g(t) \right\} \ne \mathcal{L}\left\{ f(t) \right\}\,\mathcal{L}\left\{ g(t) \right\}.]

Content:
Finally, when we apply linearity, the Laplace transform of the overall function exists only where every piece exists. So the domain of
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\}]
is the intersection of the domains of [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] and [MATH: \mathcal L\{g(t)\}.]

Content:
In the next slide, we will apply the linearity property to a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding Laplace Transforms of Sums of Exponentials

Example Prompt:
Find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{-3t}-e^{5t}] for [MATH: s>5.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity properties, we have
[MATH: L{e^{− 3t} − e^{5t}}|= L{e^{− 3t}} + L{− e^{5t}}; = L{e^{− 3t}} − L{e^{5t}}.]

Next, we recall the following result:
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k]

Therefore, we have the following:
[MATH: L{e^{− 3t}}|= (1)/(s + 3), s > − 3; L{e^{5t}}|= (1)/(s − 5), s > 5]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)] is
[MATH: L{f(t)}|= L{e^{− 3t}} − L{e^{5t}}; = (1)/(s + 3) − (1)/(s − 5); = ((s − 5) − (s + 3))/((s + 3)(s − 5)); = (− 8)/((s + 3)(s − 5)); = − (8)/((s + 3)(s − 5)).]

Finally, since [MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{-3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (-3,\infty)] and [MATH: \mathcal L \{e^{5t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (5,\infty),] we have that [MATH: \mathcal L\{f(t)\}] is defined for
[MATH: (-3,\infty) \cap (5,\infty) = (5,\infty),]
that is, [MATH: s > 5.]

---

Choices:

b. [MATH: (s + 4)/((s − 2)(s + 4))]
c. [MATH: (2s − 6)/((s + 2)(s − 4))]
d. [MATH: − (2)/((s − 2)(s + 4))]

---

d. [MATH: (2(s − 1))/(s − 5)]
e. [MATH: (s)/(s − 5)]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Laplace Transforms of Hyperbolic and Trigonometric Functions

Content:
Linearity becomes especially useful when a function can be rewritten as a linear combination of exponentials.

Content:
In particular, we can rewrite hyperbolic and trigonometric functions using exponentials:

Content:
[MATH: \cos(\omega t) = \dfrac{e^{\textrm i \omega t} + e^{-\textrm i \omega t}}{2},
\qquad
\sin(\omega t) = \dfrac{e^{\textrm i \omega t} - e^{-\textrm i \omega t}}{2\textrm i},]

Content:
[MATH: \cosh(\omega t) = \dfrac{e^{\omega t} + e^{-\omega t}}{2},
\qquad
\sinh(\omega t) = \dfrac{e^{\omega t} - e^{-\omega t}}{2}.]

Content:
Then we take the Laplace transform of both sides and apply linearity term-by-term.

Content:
To do this, we use the transforms we already know:
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{kt}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k},\qquad s > k,
\qquad\qquad
\mathcal L\{e^{\textrm i \omega t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-\textrm i \omega},\qquad s > 0.]

Content:
Note. Even though complex exponentials appear in these identities, we are still treating [MATH: s] as a real variable in this lesson.

Content:
Let's take a look at an example.

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Finding the Laplace Transform of Cosine Using Linearity

Content:
We will find the Laplace transform of [MATH: \cos(t)] by rewriting it using complex exponentials and applying linearity.

Content:
First, we recall the identity
[MATH: \cos(t) = \dfrac{e^{\mathrm{i} t} + e^{-\mathrm{i} t}}{2}.]

Content:
Now, we take the Laplace transform of both sides:
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\cos(t)\}
= \mathcal L\left\{\dfrac{e^{\mathrm{i} t} + e^{-\mathrm{i} t}}{2}\right\}.]

Content:
Next, we apply linearity:
[MATH: L{\cos (t)}|= (1)/(2)L{e^{\textrm{i}t} + e^{− \textrm{i}t}}; = (1)/(2)(L{e^{\textrm{i}t}} + L{e^{− \textrm{i}t}}).]

Content:
From the previous lesson, we know that for [MATH: s>0,]
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{\mathrm{i} \omega t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-\mathrm{i} \omega}.]
So for [MATH: \omega=1,] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{\mathrm{i} t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s-\mathrm{i}},
\qquad
\mathcal L\{e^{-\mathrm{i} t}\} = \dfrac{1}{s+\mathrm{i}}.]

Content:
Substituting these into our expression gives
[MATH: L{\cos (t)}|= (1)/(2)((1)/(s − \textrm{i}) + (1)/(s + \textrm{i})); = (1)/(2)(((s + \textrm{i}) + (s − \textrm{i}))/((s − \textrm{i})(s + \textrm{i}))); = (1)/(2)((2s)/(s^{2} − \textrm{i}^{2})); = (1)/(2)((2s)/(s^{2} + 1)); = (s)/(s^{2} + 1).]

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\cos(t)\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+1}, \qquad s>0.]

---

Item 7 — Example: Finding Laplace Transforms of Trigonometric and Hyperbolic Functions

Example Prompt:
Use the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = e^{kt}] to find the Laplace transform of [MATH: \sinh(3t).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

First, recall that, by definition
[MATH: \sinh(3t) = \dfrac{e^{3t} - e^{-3t}}{2}.]

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have
[MATH: L{\sinh (3t)}|= L{(e^{3t} − e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = L{(e^{3t})/(2) − (e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = L{(e^{3t})/(2)} − L{(e^{− 3t})/(2)}; = (1)/(2)L{e^{3t}} − (1)/(2)L{e^{− 3t}}.]

Now, we recall that
[MATH: \mathcal L\left\{e^{kt}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{s-k}, \qquad s > k.]
Therefore, we have the following:
[MATH: L{e^{3t}}|= (1)/(s − 3), s > 3; L{e^{− 3t}}|= (1)/(s + 3), s > − 3]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: \sinh(3t)] is
[MATH: L{\sinh (3t)}|= (1)/(2)L{e^{3t}} − (1)/(2)L{e^{− 3t}}; = (1)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(s − 3) − (1)/(2) ⋅ (1)/(s + 3); = (1)/(2)((1)/(s − 3) − (1)/(s + 3)); = (1)/(2)(((s + 3) − (s − 3))/((s − 3)(s + 3))); = (1)/(2)((6)/(s^{2} − 9)); = (3)/(s^{2} − 9).]

Finally, since [MATH: \mathcal L\{e^{3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (3,\infty)] and [MATH: \mathcal L \{e^{-3t}\}] is defined for [MATH: s\in (-3,\infty),] we have that [MATH: \mathcal L\{\sinh(3t)\}] is defined for
[MATH: (3,\infty) \cap (-3,\infty) = (3,\infty),]

Item 10 — Example: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions

Example Prompt:
Given that for [MATH: s > 0,]
[MATH: L{\sin ωt} = (ω)/(s^{2} + ω^{2}), L{\cos ωt} = (s)/(s^{2} + ω^{2}),]
find the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t) = 3\cos{9t} - 2\sin{9t}] for [MATH: s > 0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions [MATH: f(t)] and [MATH: g(t),] we have
[MATH: \mathcal L\{\alpha f(t) + \beta g(t)\} = \alpha\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t)\} + \beta\cdot \mathcal L \{g(t)\},]
where [MATH: \alpha] and [MATH: \beta] are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have
[MATH: L{3\cos 9t − 2\sin 9t}|= L{3\cos 9t} + L{− 2\sin 9t}; = 3L{\cos 9t} − 2L{\sin 9t}.]

We are given that
[MATH: L{\sin ωt}|= (ω)/(s^{2} + ω^{2}),|s > 0,; L{\cos ωt}|= (s)/(s^{2} + ω^{2}),|s > 0.]

Therefore, we have the following:
[MATH: L{\cos 9t}|= (s)/(s^{2} + 81), s > 0; L{\sin 9t}|= (9)/(s^{2} + 81), s > 0]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of [MATH: f(t)] is
[MATH: L{f(t)}|= 3L{\cos 9t} − 2L{\sin 9t}; = 3 ⋅ (s)/(s^{2} + 81) − 2 ⋅ (9)/(s^{2} + 81); = (3s)/(s^{2} + 81) − (18)/(s^{2} + 81); = (3s − 18)/(s^{2} + 81).]
